story.title: TikTok to Pay $400 Million in Landmark Children's Privacy Settlement
story.summary: TikTok has agreed to a $400 million settlement with the US Department of Justice following allegations that it violated children's online privacy laws. The lawsuit, filed in 2024, accused TikTok and its parent company ByteDance of collecting extensive data from users under the age of 13 without parental consent. The settlement is considered one of the largest of its kind in the United States.

explore_lenses.label: Why is this settlement significant?
explore_lenses.title: A major COPPA enforcement recovery
explore_lenses.summary: The $400 million agreement is among the largest recoveries in a U.S. children’s-privacy case and centers on whether a major social platform complied with parental-consent and deletion requirements for users under 13.

claims.text: The Justice Department described the settlement as one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a case under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).

COPPA generally requires online services that knowingly collect personal information from children under 13 to notify parents and obtain verifiable parental consent; the government’s 2024 complaint alleged TikTok collected and retained information without doing so.
The DOJ said the resolution recognizes TikTok’s claimed improvements to age-related controls, parental oversight, compliance functions, and privacy practices since the lawsuit was filed.

points: The Justice Department described the settlement as one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a case under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).

The DOJ said the resolution recognizes TikTok’s claimed improvements to age-related controls, parental oversight, compliance functions, and privacy practices since the lawsuit was filed.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The settlement resolves allegations only; the DOJ says there has been no determination of liability.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach this point?
explore_lenses.title: A follow-on case after the Musical.ly order
explore_lenses.summary: The 2024 lawsuit followed an FTC compliance review of a 2019 settlement involving TikTok predecessor Musical.ly, turning an earlier COPPA order into a new federal enforcement case.

claims.text: The FTC said its investigation began as a review of Musical.ly’s compliance with its 2019 children’s-privacy settlement, then led the commission to refer a complaint against TikTok and ByteDance to the DOJ in June 2024.
The DOJ and FTC filed the civil complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on August 2, 2024.

The complaint alleged that TikTok let children under 13 bypass its age gate, collect extensive personal information through regular accounts without parental consent, and fail in some cases to honor parents’ deletion requests.
TikTok disputed the 2024 allegations, saying at the time that many concerned past practices, were factually inaccurate, or had already been addressed.

explore_lenses.label: What still has to happen under the deal?
explore_lenses.title: The final $100 million is conditional
explore_lenses.summary: TikTok is to pay most of the settlement immediately, but the remaining portion is tied to a court order vacating the predecessor company’s consent decree—making the court process consequential even after the announced agreement.

claims.text: Under the DOJ’s announced terms, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and another $100 million when a court enters an order vacating the prior consent decree against Musical.ly.

The original 2024 case sought civil penalties and injunctive relief, but the DOJ’s settlement announcement emphasizes the payment and says TikTok has already implemented measures intended to improve protections for younger users.

Children’s-advocacy group Fairplay argues that vacating the 2019 order would remove obligations beyond baseline legal requirements; this is the group’s assessment, not a finding in the DOJ announcement.

story_report.summary: TikTok and parent company ByteDance have agreed to a $400 million resolution of a U.S. Justice Department children’s-privacy lawsuit filed in 2024. The government had alleged violations of the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, including collecting and retaining personal information from children under 13 without required parental notice and verifiable consent. Under the announced terms, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately, with a further $100 million due when a court vacates an earlier consent decree involving Musical.ly. The resolution contains no determination of liability.

sections.heading: TikTok Case Origins and Allegations
sections.body: The Federal Trade Commission’s inquiry began as a review of Musical.ly’s compliance with its 2019 children’s-privacy settlement and resulted in a June 2024 referral to the Justice Department. DOJ and FTC then filed their civil complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on August 2, 2024. The complaint alleged that children could bypass TikTok’s age gate, use regular accounts that collected extensive personal information without parental consent, and in some cases have parents’ deletion requests ignored.

sections.heading: TikTok Settlement Terms and Safeguards
sections.body: The Justice Department called the agreement one of the largest recoveries ever obtained under COPPA, which generally requires services knowingly collecting children’s personal information to notify parents and obtain verifiable consent. DOJ said the resolution recognizes TikTok’s claimed improvements to age controls, parental oversight, compliance functions and privacy practices since the case began. TikTok had disputed the 2024 allegations, saying many concerned past practices, were inaccurate or had already been addressed. Fairplay, a children’s-advocacy group, argues that vacating the Musical.ly order could remove obligations exceeding baseline legal requirements.

unresolved.text: The public Justice Department announcement does not specify which allegations TikTok accepted or disputed in reaching the settlement.
As of August 22, 2026, the Justice Department had not published a court vacatur order or a full settlement text detailing any continuing compliance, monitoring or reporting requirements.

related_stories.title: Canada to Retaliate with Equal Tariffs Following US Trade Dispute
related_stories.summary: After failing to reach a trade agreement, the United States has imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada will match these tariffs 'dollar for dollar' to protect its workers and businesses. The trade tensions mark a significant escalation in relations between the two countries.

related_stories.title: Fatal Sword Attack at Swedish School Leaves One Dead and Three Injured
related_stories.summary: A sword attack at a high school in Fagersta, central Sweden, resulted in one death and three injuries. The victim was a 17-year-old girl. An 18-year-old male suspect has been arrested following the incident, which occurred as schools reopened in the area. Police are investigating potential online influences that may have incited the attack.

related_stories.title: Supreme Court Temporarily Allows Construction of $400 Million White House Ballroom
related_stories.summary: The US Supreme Court has granted a temporary order allowing the continuation of construction on a $400 million ballroom at the White House, a project associated with President Donald Trump. This decision comes after lower courts had previously ordered a halt to the work, citing the need for congressional approval. The ruling provides a temporary victory for the Trump administration as it navigates ongoing legal challenges regarding the renovation.

related_stories.title: Pentagon Dismisses Leadership of Stars and Stripes Amid Editorial Independence Concerns
related_stories.summary: The Pentagon has dismissed the editor-in-chief, publisher, and a reporter of Stars and Stripes, citing insubordination. The firings occurred after the editor and reporter publicly opposed potential editorial interference from the Defense Department. This action raises concerns about the independence of the military news outlet, which has a history of editorial autonomy.
